channel.title: The Missing Seat
channel.description: Evidence-based editorials asking who is missing, why it matters, and what can be done.

item.title: The Absence Rate Was Over 100%. The Oversight Had Already Stopped.
item.description: At least one in four students has been chronically absent. But the federal data used to track the problem can produce rates above 100 percent, and the Education Department stopped its most comprehensive oversight of the programs carrying nearly $27 billion.

item.title: The Water Project Was Built. The Missing Money Was for Keeping It Alive.
item.description: Washington likes to cut the ribbon when a water system is built. A new federal audit shows what happens when the rules do not cover every home and the money to keep the system working is treated as somebody else’s problem.

item.title: The Efficiency Team Got Access. The Public Still Cannot See the Security Receipt.
item.description: GAO could not verify the full access or safeguards because six agencies supplied incomplete records. This is an assurance gap, not proof of a breach.

item.title: The HR Manager Said No to Discrimination. Then She Allegedly Lost Her Job.
item.description: An equal-opportunity policy means little if the person expected to defend it can be punished for speaking.

item.title: They Served the United States. The Nearest VA Care May Be an Ocean Away.
item.description: Citizens of three Pacific nations can enlist in the U.S. military. But after they return home, VA healthcare may require an international flight without VA travel reimbursement.

item.title: They Trusted Black Women With Their Babies. Just Not With Power.
item.description: America trusted Black women with intimate responsibilities, including caring for white children. But trust in their labor did not become equal protection, fair pay or equal power.

item.title: The Campaign Was the Ad. We’re Stuck With the Bill.
item.description: American candidates can promise tax cuts, new programs and sweeping savings without giving voters one independent receipt for the whole plan. Australia already shows that another way is possible.

item.title: Trump and Black America: What Helped, What Hurt, and What Will Last?
item.description: A plain-language ledger of what changed, who gained, who lost, what is temporary, what is law, and whether the Black-white gap actually narrowed.

item.title: Dear World: Before You Tell Me How Great America Is, Tell the Whole Story
item.description: America can celebrate what it built without hiding who paid for it. If the world wants to understand this country, it has to meet all of us, not just the America in the commercial.

item.title: The Robe Doesn’t Erase What the Judge Knows
item.description: A judge’s recorded prejudice raises a question retirement alone cannot answer: What happened in the cases she already decided?

item.title: “Black-on-Black Crime”: Naming the Violence Without Hiding Its History
item.description: Violence within Black communities is real. So is the history that shaped where violence, poverty and disadvantage became concentrated.

item.title: What Can We Do to Make Justice Happen?
item.description: If injustice was built through laws, institutions and public choices, what can be done now?

item.title: The Class Construction After Reconstruction
item.description: Emancipation ended slavery. It did not erase the economic and social hierarchy built around it.

item.title: Nigger: The Word, the Law and the Line We Draw
item.description: The public often punishes America’s most infamous racial slur more readily than the hierarchy the word declares.

item.title: Power Is Not Proof of Superiority
item.description: Centuries of oppression prove that domination can be organized and preserved. They do not prove a racial hierarchy.

item.title: The Violence Behind the Reconstruction Amendments
item.description: The doctrine cannot be separated from the murders, rape, torture, massacres and political terror that constitutional protection was meant to confront.
